item.title: Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy
item.description:
Imagination

Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

Literary characters' sense of self-worth can convey the humanity of others.

Posted November 21, 2026

Key points
  • Literary characters can "cross over" into readers' lives, becoming an enduring presence.
  • Characters who linger can inspire readers if they share experiences rarely described in published work.
  • Researchers can learn from authors' depictions of people underrepresented in psychological experiments.

What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

Austin Schmid, Joyful Sunset, 3 October 2015
Source: Austin Schmid (schmidy), Joyful Sunset, 3 October 2015, Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication

In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

When characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

Born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to New Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

Recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

Junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger shows not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

Like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

item.title: Nihilism Is Not What You Think
item.description:
Philosophy

Nihilism Is Not What You Think

Denying cosmic meaning does not imply despair or immorality.

Posted November 21, 2026

Key points
  • Existential nihilism says life has no built-in purpose, though it doesn't cause self-destructive behavior.
  • Moral nihilism rejects built-in right and wrong, which doesn't mean people act immorally.
  • Existentialism starts with a purposeless universe and explores why people still crave meaning.

Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism. Nihilism, often used as a derogatory term for a "life-denying," destructive, and perhaps most of all depressive philosophy, is what drove existentialists to write about the right response to a meaningless universe devoid of purpose. This is why I've published an academic article on the topic. As nihilism is commonly used as a derogatory term, even in the works of Friedrich Nietzsche, it will prove helpful for the purpose of this post to take a "value-neutral" view on nihilism and achieve conceptual clarity of the term nihilism, beyond some sort of "life-denying" philosophy.

Moral and Existential Nihilism

I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values. Moral nihilism, therefore, refers to the meta-ethical thesis that there is no objective morality, no inherent goodness or wrongness, a view that many existentialists agree with. The concern here, however, is existential nihilism, which can be defined as the denial of life being meaningful and the universe having a purpose. Whether moral and existential nihilism entail each other is beyond the scope of this post, but they at least stand in a close relation.

Existentialists are by definition, therefore, all existential nihilists, though not necessarily moral nihilists or atheists. As is commonly joked about existentialist thinkers, with the exception of Sartre, they do not appreciate being labelled as existentialists. Just like moral nihilism is often negatively associated and equated with immoralism, existential nihilism is often associated with destructive behaviour and suicide. These positions, however, should not be confused or seen as standing in a necessary causal relationship.

Existential nihilism, despite its negative connotations, should therefore not be seen as a label, but rather as something that is taken as a fact or at least a widespread view in the modern world, from which existential philosophy takes off. The popularity and critical acclaim of contemporary works such as BoJack Horseman, True Detective, and Rick and Morty exploring existential nihilism make it one of the most popular philosophical views in folk philosophy.

Not Just for Existentialists

In his defence of scientism, Alex Rosenberg makes the case that many of “life’s persistent questions” can be answered by science, among them: “Is there a God? No. […] What is the purpose of the universe? There is none. What is the meaning of life? Ditto. Why am I here? Just dumb luck.” It is no coincidence that these answers closely mimic the diagnosis provided by (the atheists among) existentialist thinkers. This line of argument is common in at least the atheistic tradition of existentialism.

article continues after advertisement

But in the face of evil and chaos, it is questionable whether, even with the existence of a supposed deity, our lives are bestowed with any meaning. Theistic existentialists like Kierkegaard, Shestov, and Jaspers would deny such.

The absurd stems from the fact that though life is without meaning and the universe devoid of purpose, man still longs for meaning, significance, and purpose. For existential thinkers like Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, this conflict was central to their philosophy.

item.title: How to Have a Difficult Conversation With Your Friend
item.description:
Friends

How to Have a Difficult Conversation With Your Friend

Here's how you can have the tough conversation without complicating your bond.

Posted November 21, 2026

Key points
  • Specific examples, rather than broad accusations, keep tough talks focused on solutions.
  • Pairing “I” statements with a friend's perspective helps reduce the risk of escalating conflict.
  • Explaining how a friend's actions affect one's feelings takes the focus off of what the friend did wrong.
Source: Liza Summer / Pexels

There is no such thing as a healthy relationship without healthy communication, whether it’s romantic, familial, or platonic. The significance of open and honest conversations in relationships cannot be overstated. In the context of friendships, where camaraderie and shared experiences lay the foundation, the ability to engage in difficult dialogue becomes even more crucial.

While the good times create cherished memories, it’s the ability to weather storms that truly defines the strength of a friendship. Hard conversations offer a unique opportunity for growth, both individually and collectively. They enable friends to address issues head-on, clear up misunderstandings, and build a foundation of trust that can withstand the test of time.

Challenging conversations, though daunting, are pivotal for personal and relational growth. Here are three practical ways to navigate difficult conversations successfully in a friendship.

1. Back Your Point With Strong Evidence

Before initiating a hard conversation, it’s essential to gather solid evidence to support your concerns. Evidence can make it easier for your friend to understand the gravity of the situation.

Be specific about incidents or behaviors that fuel your concerns and approach the conversation with a non-confrontational attitude. Researchers utilizing discursive psychology and conversational analysis assert that attending to small details can significantly impact interactions, emphasizing how the formulation of an idea can dramatically alter the conversation’s direction.

To avoid turning molehills into mountains, offer examples illustrating your observations. Instead of saying, “You’ve been distant lately,” convey, “I noticed that we haven’t spent much time together in the past few weeks and our communication has become less frequent.” This specific and non-accusatory approach helps your friend see the tangible actions contributing to the issue.

Presenting evidence in a clear and organized manner enables both parties to focus on the issue at hand, steering the conversation away from blame and toward a more productive, solution-oriented dialogue.

2. Turn on the Impact Radar

It’s essential to help your friend comprehend the impact of their actions on their relationships, no matter how difficult the conversation. If any of your friend’s actions affect you, express your concerns in terms of emotions and outcomes. Emotional context will help your friend connect with your perspective on a deeper level.

Numerous studies suggest that incorporating both self- and other-perspective using I-language is an effective strategy for initiating discussions that could lead to conflict. This approach significantly reduces the likelihood of discussions laden with conflict escalating into a negative spiral of hostility.

So, take the time to articulate how their actions have affected you, using “I” statements. Instead of saying, “You always cancel plans,” express, “When plans get canceled frequently, I feel undervalued, and it affects the trust I have in our commitments to each other.” This method communicates the impact without levying blame, creating an atmosphere conducive to constructive dialogue.

Additionally, highlight the potential long-term consequences of certain behaviors on the friendship. Discuss how unaddressed patterns of behavior could strain the connection between both of you, encouraging empathy and a deeper understanding of the need for change. Remember, laying the groundwork for positive transformation involves collaboratively exploring solutions that benefit both parties.

3. Test the Waters Before Taking the Plunge

Approaching a challenging conversation can feel overwhelming, and diving headfirst into the meat of the matter may not always be the best strategy. Instead, consider taking small, gradual steps. Start by addressing minor issues or concerns.

Initiate the conversation by expressing your thoughts on less critical topics in an affirming manner, allowing both parties to acclimate to discussing challenging subjects. This gradual approach serves as an emotional warm-up, creating a comfortable space for open communication. If you observe a positive change in communication patterns, you can begin to broach more specific and sensitive instances and how they made you feel.

Taking these measured steps not only allows you and your friend to ease into the conversation but also establishes a foundation for addressing more complex issues. This incremental process contributes to a sense of safety and trust, demonstrating a commitment to understanding each other’s perspectives without immediate judgment or fear of criticism or rejection.

Friendship interventions have the potential to propel you toward personal growth, and approaching challenging dialogues with empathy, understanding, and a commitment to growth can elevate your friendships to new heights. Begin by taking these small steps, and keep in mind that the discomfort of engaging in a difficult conversation is a modest price to pay for the resilience and depth it brings to your bonds.

item.title: Facing Fears in Huntington's Disease
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Facing Fears in Huntington's Disease

Personal Perspective: Caught between avoidance and confrontation.

Posted November 21, 2026

Every now and then, I get an automated message in my inbox telling me it’s been a while since I’ve tended to my blog:

Dear Pamela Mallette LCPC, It's been 90 days or longer since you last posted to Living With Huntington's Disease on Psychology Today. We miss your voice in the mix.

Too bad, I think. It’s not that I’m trying to be rude, and it’s not that I have nothing to say (ask anyone). It’s just that I look forward to writing about my bad brain about as much as I look forward to sticking my head in a blender.

Don’t get me wrong: I enjoy the writing process. It’s the subject matter that irks me. Being gene-positive for Huntington’s Disease (HD) means I am facing down one of the cruelest diseases known to humankind, and writing about it can be a real downer. There’s a great weight off when I finish a post, and I feel free to live my life without thinking about it again.

I rest, gloriously.

The Dance of Death

But sooner than I’d like, the email comes along, and with it the invitation to return to the matter of my doom. It forces me out of hibernation and into the spasmodic dance between Avoidance and Confrontation: the Death Tango, as I like to call it—fear and courage, in their epic entanglement within my psyche.

Source: Guren-The-Thirdeye / Pixabay

Avoidance, in its protective wisdom, tells me to ignore the emails and let the blog go dark. It’s not worth it. It’s too heavy, and you have enough going on. Spend your time on something—anything—else. Not bad advice. After all, there’s no real pressure, no real consequence, if I don’t write.

It feels like safety to avoid. Unfortunately, ignoring it doesn’t get me very far. I can delete an email or neglect a blog, but I can’t erase my DNA. Nor can I ignore the inheritability of this disease (50 percent), which means my children are at risk. Avoidance would leave all of us unprepared for realities to come, and I’m unwilling to do that.

Plus, as a therapist, I know that facing my reality is probably good for me, or whatever.

So I let Confrontation take the lead, if only because there is no other choice. I follow that valorous fool into dangerous territory, where the different faces of HD lurk around dark corners, each triggering their own primal fears within me.

Dangers Untold, Hardships Unnumbered (But I'll Stick to Three)

The most common face of HD is chorea, the involuntary, dance-like motor symptoms that take away a person’s physical autonomy. But it goes further. In later stages, HD breaks you down until you are wheelchair-bound, bedridden, and unable to feed, dress, or bathe yourself.

The loss of physical independence is devastating, but that’s not the worst part for me. The world can be a very unkind place for people with physical challenges, and that’s where the fear sets in. Being on the receiving end of ridicule or humiliation when I am defenseless and vulnerable is literally my worst nightmare.

Then there’s the emotional and psychological decline. Because of damage to the caudate nucleus and frontal lobes, behaviors and emotions start to change as the disease progresses. Once caring people become apathetic. Relaxed people become obsessive and demanding. The gentle become irritable and enraged.

What does this mean for me? Am I not going to be funny anymore? Will I be rude to people for no reason? What if I turn into someone I can’t stand? There’s no telling who I will become as the disease progresses, and my soul shudders.

And of course, there’s the death part. It’s not the dying itself that scares me; it’s that HD, that Biological Robber Baron, claims entire decades as it disrupts the natural lifespan. It most commonly manifests during midlife, such that you become incapacitated in your prime adult living years, and often don’t see your golden years at all.

These are significant periods of time that I have been looking forward to. But if my trajectory is typical, I’m not going to have the future I want. Instead, only the stark sorrow that my best days may be already behind me.

See what I mean? Head, blender.

So how do I do this? How do I face the darkness without being overcome by it?

A Message From the Beyond

Recently someone close to me told me about a memorial service he’d attended. Though he didn’t know the deceased personally, by all accounts the man being mourned lived an incredible life that touched everyone he encountered for the better.

Source: OpenClipart-Vectors / Pixabay

In memorializing her father, his daughter told of a note she found after his death, something he’d scribbled down and posted on a mirror. It had just three words: “purpose without pressure.”

How simple, and how deep, was this man’s wisdom. He didn’t know it, but with those words he was providing my problem with a solution: balance.

Because just as there is fear, there is meaning—purpose—as well. There’s therapeutic value to voicing the fears, because I don’t often speak them aloud (tends to bring down the mood at parties). And of course, there’s the hope that this writing might encourage someone in the HD community, or that it might help those outside the community to have more understanding and empathy.

Perhaps my greatest purpose is this: If HD is going to take my voice from me, then I will use it as long as possible. Where it destroys, I create. I can try to bring some beauty to this journey, even when all I can say is that I hate it and I’m scared.

So yes, I choose to lean into purpose. But because it’s so grave, I heed the advice of the dead. I give myself permission to honor the enormity of the task by taking my time, coming to it only gently, when I am ready. I write from flow, not force, and I release expectation of the outcome.

Purpose. Without pressure.

Thank you, Peter Vlasses. May you rest in your way, and I in mine.

item.title: How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?
item.description:
Relationships

How Long Should We Wait for Sex, Cohabitation, and Marriage?

Romantic patience matters more than following a timetable.

Posted November 21, 2026

Key points
  • Active patience is more valuable than passive waiting.
  • Cohabitation works best when guided by commitment rather than convenience.
  • The path to marriage matters less than the relationship built along the way.
Source: pexels-michelle-leman-6765727

"Wise men say, 'Only fools rush in,' but I can't help falling in love with you." — Elvis Presley

How long should you wait before having sex? Moving in together? Getting married? These are among the most common questions people ask about romantic relationships. Yet there is no magical timeline that guarantees success. The value of waiting depends on the partners, their circumstances, and the nature of their relationship. Still, one principle often proves valuable: patience.

Patience Is Not the Same as Waiting

"Patience is not simply the ability to wait. It's how we behave while we're waiting." — Joyce Meyer

There's a crucial distinction between waiting and patience. Waiting is passive: Time passes while little changes. Patience, by contrast, is active. It involves investing in the relationship while recognizing that some developments should not be rushed. Patience creates the conditions for intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen naturally. Unlike procrastination, which unnecessarily delays action, patience reflects wise timing. The important question is not how long we wait, but whether we practice patience rather than merely let time pass (Ben‐Ze'ev, 2019; and here).

How Long Should You Wait for Sex?

"I don't have a set time frame for sex, but it's always before it gets super serious. I've got to test-drive the car before buying it." — A woman

"My boyfriend and I had sex on the first date, and we're still together a year later and talking about getting engaged soon. The right person isn't going to think less of you because of the speedy sex." — A woman

Sexual attraction is a defining feature of romantic love, making the timing of sexual intimacy especially significant. Research often finds that couples who delay sex report greater relationship quality and lower breakup rates. Waiting may allow emotional intimacy and communication to develop before physical intimacy takes center stage. Some studies suggest that couples who wait several months before becoming sexually involved report greater satisfaction and relationship stability (Vancour & Fallon, 2017).

Yet these findings do not mean that sex on the first date is a mistake. What matters most is not the calendar but the context. Partners differ in their values, attachment styles, and goals. For some well-matched couples, early sexual intimacy may strengthen their initial bond. The important question is therefore not, "How many dates should we wait?" but "Are we both comfortable with the pace at which intimacy is developing?"

How Long Should Couples Cohabit Before Marriage?

"With love and patience, nothing is impossible." — Daisaku Ikeda

Premarital cohabitation has become the norm for most American couples. Yet living together can serve very different purposes.

Research suggests that couples who move in together mainly to "test" the relationship are more likely to break up than those who cohabit because they genuinely want to spend more time together (Chapman et al., 2026). One reason is that living together creates practical and financial interdependence, making it harder to evaluate the relationship objectively. Couples who move in together after discussing long-term plans, or after becoming engaged, generally report better marital outcomes than those who simply drift into cohabitation because it feels convenient.

Researchers therefore distinguish between sliding into cohabitation and deciding to cohabit. Sliding involves little deliberate discussion or commitment; deciding reflects conscious consideration of the relationship's future. Indeed, more than half of cohabiting couples report that they had not explicitly discussed moving in together before doing so. The central issue is not whether couples should live together before marriage, but whether cohabitation expresses mutual commitment and thoughtful deliberation rather than uncertainty and inertia.

How Long Should You Date Before Marriage?

"The ideal amount of time to date before getting married is at least a whole year. It's crazy to marry someone before you've seen what they're like in winter." — A woman

No dating duration can guarantee marital success. Nevertheless, many relationship researchers and therapists suggest that two to three years often provides enough time to know a partner across different circumstances while preserving romantic momentum.

Dating typically differs from hooking up because it is part of a broader process of building an enduring relationship. Yet the distinction is far from absolute. Many successful relationships begin as casual encounters. One-night stands sometimes become lifelong partnerships, and dating apps such as Tinder, often criticized for promoting casual sex, have also become important pathways to marriage. The route matters less than what develops along the way.

The Real Value of Romantic Patience

"Lovers are patient and know that the moon needs time to become full." — Rumi

Love has no universally correct timetable. There are no strict rules governing when to have sex, how long to live together, or how long to date before marriage. What matters is not simply how long partners wait before taking the next step, but whether they use that time wisely. Passive waiting merely allows the clock to advance; active patience allows intimacy, trust, and commitment to deepen. Romantic flourishing depends less on the passage of time than on what partners do with it.
